title: Reliable communication and computer control after profound paralysis

concept.text: The innovation is dependable, self-directed communication and computer control for people who have lost speech and most voluntary movement. A brain–computer interface would translate neural signals associated with intended speech or device actions into communication and computer input. The intended advance is sustained, useful access in ordinary life: expressing thoughts, operating applications, and managing interaction without continual assistance from researchers. The supplied publisher summary describes substantial progress toward this outcome in one participant using an intracortical interface for speech and cursor control.

Proposed scope: a practical interface should support error correction, expressive communication, and deliberate control over when decoding starts and stops. It should accommodate different users and changing needs while remaining usable over years with manageable setup and support. Surgery-free operation could broaden applicability, but it is not required for this concept. These are proposed requirements for dependable access, rather than capabilities all established by the supplied evidence.

significance.text: If dependable access could be extended across many people with profound paralysis, it would overcome a major barrier to personal agency. The direct consequences would be the ability to communicate intentions and choices and to control computer-mediated activities despite severe movement and speech impairment. The publisher summary connects loss of speech and device control with reduced independence and quality of life, and its reported home-use demonstration provides a concrete technical basis for this conditional impact.

Impact synthesis: broader participation in work, relationships, and personal decisions would remain conditional on affordability, support, accessible software, and accommodation. Independence from researchers can coexist with assistance from trained care partners; it should not be interpreted as complete freedom from help. The revolutionary threshold is dependable access for many people in ordinary circumstances. Communication and cursor control also do not, by themselves, establish restoration of movement, unrestricted access to thoughts, neural writing, or memory transfer.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unresolved capability is extending high-performance speech and computer-control interfaces into consistently dependable everyday use across users. The supplied summary identifies wider applicability, portability, and consistently high accuracy during natural conversation as remaining challenges. A substantial demonstration in one participant establishes feasibility in that setting, but leaves open how reliably the approach transfers to other people and circumstances.

Engineering synthesis: the system must handle differences among users, diagnoses, degrees of impairment, and recording conditions, as well as possible changes over time. Concrete proposed requirements include maintaining decoding performance with little setup, recovering from errors, making correction accessible to someone with very limited movement, and preserving a user's intended expression. Deliberate activation and deactivation are also necessary design goals for self-directed use. The supplied summary does not quantify these challenges or establish that each has been solved.

Practical and biomedical synthesis: an implanted implementation also requires durable neural recording, acceptable surgical and long-term implant safety, maintainable equipment, and a support arrangement that users and care partners can sustain. Reliable application control must work alongside communication rather than making ordinary tasks depend on repeated specialist intervention. These are proposed barriers to broad deployment; the supplied summary does not provide a complete safety record, long-term maintenance burden, or comparison of implanted and surgery-free approaches.

current_state.text: A meaningful everyday-use threshold has been demonstrated for one participant, according to the supplied publisher summary. It identifies Nicholas S. Card, T. Singer-Clark, H. Peracha, and colleagues’ article, “Long-term independent use of an intracortical brain–computer interface for speech and cursor control,” published in Nature Medicine on 15 June 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41591-026-04414-6. The publisher summary, dated 16 June 2026, reports more than 3,800 hours of near-daily home use over almost two years. It reports 183,060 sentences, almost two million words, and an average communication rate of 56 words per minute.

The summary describes operation without researcher assistance, with trained care partners. This is substantial evidence of sustained use outside a laboratory, while retaining an important distinction between researcher independence and absence of assistance. The report concerns one participant and explicitly identifies wider applicability, improved portability, and consistently high accuracy during natural conversation as areas requiring further work. The reported average communication rate therefore should not be read as proof of uniformly accurate, effortless conversation in all settings.

Evidence boundary: these details come from the supplied review of the publisher’s research summary. The retained summary was complete and untruncated, with no extraction issues recorded, but the journal article itself was not supplied for inspection. Consequently, the full methods, participant characteristics, error measures, safety findings, and performance distributions cannot be assessed here. The summary supports “almost two years”; the earlier “roughly 19 months” cannot be verified from this material. These limits do not negate the reported demonstration, but they constrain its interpretation.

Coverage limitation: the supplied material contains no bounded freshness search establishing the field’s state as of 1 November 2026 or identifying developments after the June report. This record therefore describes the dated achievement supported by the supplied evidence and does not claim an exhaustive account of subsequent progress.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: independently evaluate multi-year use by multiple people with different diagnoses and degrees of impairment in homes and, where relevant, workplaces. Participants should conduct spontaneous conversations, operate ordinary applications, correct errors through an accessible method, and intentionally start and stop decoding. Evaluate how these activities work without routine researcher intervention, while recording any care-partner assistance. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent multi-year communication and computer control across diverse participants

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement and reproducibility requirements: report communication rate together with accuracy, correction time, conversational success, application-task completion, setup time, interruptions, and changes in performance over time. Describe participant selection, training, calibration, hardware and software, and the assistance required so that independent teams can assess and reproduce the result. Sustained success should be evaluated across participants and settings, with individual outcomes visible rather than obscured by averages.
completion_criteria.label: Report reproducible methods and individual performance across participants and settings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report adverse events, equipment failures, maintenance requirements, care-partner training and workload, and access costs alongside performance. State which activities users can perform themselves and which require assistance. A convincing result would demonstrate useful breadth across the evaluated population and circumstances; finite testing cannot establish literal universality across every diagnosis, user, or future condition. The proposed evaluation directly addresses the wider-applicability, portability, and natural-conversation limitations identified in the publisher summary.
completion_criteria.label: Report safety, practical burdens, and limits of demonstrated applicability

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: HCI-01, “A predictive science of human–computer interaction,” could inform how to predict usability, learning demands, and interaction performance for these interfaces. HCI-02 concerns delivering dependable access after profound paralysis; HCI-01 concerns a broader scientific ability to predict interaction outcomes. HCI-04, “An interface that makes inaccessible software operable through a user’s chosen modality,” overlaps in the goal of making ordinary software usable. HCI-02 supplies communication and input capabilities despite paralysis, while HCI-04 addresses software accessibility across chosen modalities. Their combination could be useful, but neither capability establishes the other.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-03, “A general-purpose, high-fidelity interface for touch and physical force,” and HCI-07, “Everyday visual computing with perceptually convincing spatial displays,” concern other interaction channels. HCI-02 does not require high-fidelity touch, force feedback, or spatial displays. It may use conventional visual or other feedback, while its defining outcome remains reliable communication and computer control.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-05, “End-user programming that ordinary users can understand and maintain,” concerns users creating and maintaining software behavior. HCI-06, “Delegation interfaces that keep people in meaningful control of computer work,” concerns directing and overseeing delegated activity. A person could use HCI-02 to access either kind of interface, but decoding intended communication or cursor actions does not itself solve understandable programming or meaningful supervision of delegated work.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-08, “Real-time conversational interfaces across signed and spoken languages,” and HCI-11, “Remote collaboration with usable shared social and spatial cues,” overlap with communication and participation. HCI-02 addresses access when speech and movement are profoundly impaired; HCI-08 addresses communication across languages and modalities, and HCI-11 addresses the cues that make remote collaboration usable. Successful neural speech decoding alone does not establish language translation or shared social and spatial presence.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-09, “Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services,” is relevant to handling sensitive interface data and user control. HCI-02 includes deliberate control over decoding as a proposed requirement, but does not establish enforceable privacy across services. HCI-10, “Lifelong personal memory augmentation with controllable evidence,” concerns retaining and retrieving personal information with evidence control. Restoring communication and computer input does not demonstrate memory augmentation or memory upload.

Scope synthesis: the research also mentions a historical bidirectional BCI proposal, but that proposal was not supplied for comparison. Communication is the stated point of overlap. HCI-02 does not require writing information into the nervous system or transferring memories; no stronger claim about the historical proposal’s scope can be established from these inputs.

unresolved_issues: The full journal article was not supplied, leaving detailed methods, participant characteristics, accuracy measures, safety findings, and performance variability unassessed.
The precise usage duration underlying “almost two years” remains unresolved; the earlier 19-month figure is not verified by the supplied summary.
Generalization across people, diagnoses, degrees of impairment, and longer periods remains unresolved by the single-participant demonstration.
The supplied material does not quantify portability, care-partner workload, maintenance demands, access costs, or consistently achievable natural-conversation accuracy.
No bounded freshness search establishes developments after June 2026 or completeness as of 1 November 2026.
The historical bidirectional BCI proposal was not supplied, so its relationship to HCI-02 cannot be assessed beyond the limited comparison preserved here.

brief.title: Dependable communication after profound paralysis
possible: People who cannot speak or move could hold conversations, express choices and use ordinary computer applications for years without continual researcher help. A device would turn brain signals for intended speech or actions into words and computer input.
Users could correct mistakes, preserve expression in their voice and decide when the system listens. Communication and computer control would become dependable parts of daily life.
why: For people with profound paralysis, dependable access would restore more control over relationships, work and personal decisions. They could communicate intentions and take part in activities that otherwise depend on someone interpreting or carrying out their wishes.

sources.showed: A participant used a brain implant for speech-based communication and computer control at home for almost two years. Trained care partners operated it without researcher assistance.
sources.quote: Neural signals recorded from implanted electrode arrays in the speech motor cortex of the brain were decoded in real time into text and cursor control.
sources.cited_for: The study supports sustained communication and computer use outside a laboratory.
sources.not_established: It does not establish dependable performance across users or consistently accurate natural conversation.

sources.showed: A person with progressive paralysis used an implanted communication device independently at home for seven years. Use ended as brain signals weakened.
sources.quote: At-home use ended when control of the brain-computer interface became unreliable. No signs of technical malfunction were found.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates long-lasting home communication and documents its eventual loss of reliability.
sources.not_established: It does not establish that communication remains dependable as the underlying disease progresses.

sources.showed: A brain implant turned attempted speech into an artificial voice that a participant could hear immediately. He could change intonation and sing short melodies.
sources.quote: The resulting synthesized voice was often (but not consistently) intelligible and human listeners were able to identify the words with high accuracy.
sources.cited_for: The study supports expressive voice output rather than communication through text alone.
sources.not_established: Speech was not consistently understandable, and the study did not establish lasting independent everyday use.

sources.showed: Their CORP software kept a brain implant's translation of attempted handwriting into text accurate by updating it during use.
sources.quote:
CORP achieved a stable decoding accuracy of 93.84% in an
online handwriting iBCI task, significantly outperforming other baseline methods.
sources.cited_for: The study supports adapting to changing brain signals without separate retraining sessions.
sources.not_established: Monthly sentence-copying tests with a participant did not establish independent everyday use.

shown: Card and colleagues demonstrated combined communication and computer control during near-daily home use. The participant averaged 56 words per minute. Other teams have demonstrated longer-lasting communication alone, expressive artificial speech and software that adapts to changing brain signals.
missing: Dependable communication and application control across people with different diagnoses and degrees of impairment remain unproven.
Everyday use still needs accessible error correction, deliberate starting and stopping, and consistently accurate conversation.
Durable implants, portable equipment and manageable setup, maintenance and care-partner support need broader demonstration.

milestones.label: Diverse users sustain independent communication and computer control
milestones.explanation: People with different impairments would have to converse, use applications, correct errors and start and stop decoding over years in everyday settings, with assistance documented. This would establish dependable access beyond isolated cases.

milestones.label: Reproducible methods reveal each user's everyday performance
milestones.explanation: Teams would have to report reproducible methods and individual results for accuracy, speed, corrections, task success and support across settings and time. This would reveal whether success extends beyond favorable averages.

milestones.label: Safety, practical burdens and applicability become clear
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to document safety, failures, upkeep, costs and care-partner workload alongside performance and who benefits. This would establish practical usefulness and clarify which activities still require help.

uncertain: It remains unclear how performance will change as users' conditions and brain signals change.
The accuracy consistently achievable in natural conversation remains uncertain.
The acceptable balance between independence, care-partner assistance and practical burden remains open.

page.title: Implanted brain–computer interfaces for communication and control
page.definition: Implanted electrodes record brain activity as a person with severe paralysis tries to speak or move. Software converts those signals into text, synthesized speech or computer commands. A user can, for example, point with an eye tracker and click with a brain signal. One participant has used an investigational system for both communication and computer control at home. The goal is an implant approved for those home uses, with any required assistance specified.

goal.need: In a US survey of 216 people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), 36 reported being unable to speak. One man with ALS typed 6.3 words per minute with a head mouse. Eye tracking can also become unreliable as voluntary eye control declines. A person who can still produce a reliable brain signal can converse with family, send email and use a computer for work at home. A caregiver may still need to position the equipment and turn it on.

figures.caption: Communication rates reported for one participant with ALS
figures.note: Interpreter and head-mouse measurements preceded implantation. The BCI value is the mean during personal use; this was not a randomized comparison.

statements.quote: The aim of the PRIME Study is to demonstrate that the Link is safe and useful in daily life.
statements.context: The Link is an implanted BCI being investigated for computer control by people with quadriplegia.

statements.body: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, cooperative agreement U01DC016686
statements.quote: develop faster and more versatile BCI control techniques for home use
statements.context: The funded project’s abstract names point-and-click computer control and speech synthesis as aims for people with locked-in syndrome.

completion.title: FDA grants premarket approval for an implanted BCI for home communication and computer control.
completion.criterion: An FDA premarket approval decision authorizes an implanted BCI for communication and computer control at home in people with severe paralysis. The evidence establishes safety and effectiveness for those intended uses, and the approved labeling covers the home setting, intended users and required assistance. An investigational device exemption permits research and does not satisfy this test.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, premarket approval framework; home-use considerations in its implanted BCI guidance.
completion.threshold_quote: The applicant must receive FDA approval of its PMA application prior to marketing the device.
completion.basis: Premarket approval requires sufficient valid scientific evidence of safety and effectiveness for the intended uses. Applying that decision to home communication and computer control makes the clinical indication explicit. FDA’s BCI guidance calls for evaluation in realistic home environments and assessment of caregiver assistance. This is a US regulatory completion test.

milestones.title: FDA and the site’s institutional review board authorize the implant’s first US study in people.
milestones.criterion: For a significant-risk US study, the sponsor obtains FDA approval of an investigational device exemption and approval of the investigation from the institutional review board at each participating site before the study begins. The evidence from prior investigations and the risk controls are specific to the device.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, IDE approval requirements and implanted BCI nonclinical guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: Studies of devices that pose a significant risk require both FDA and an Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval prior to initiation of a clinical study.

milestones.title: An implanted BCI enables a person with paralysis to control a computer in an early feasibility study.
milestones.criterion: An early feasibility study evaluates initial clinical safety and shows that a person with paralysis can intentionally issue a computer command using a signal from the implant. A neural click used to select an item qualifies when an eye tracker supplies pointer movement. The study must identify the action controlled by the implant.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Early Feasibility Studies Program; clinical proof of concept demonstrated in the cited studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: initial clinical safety and device functionality

milestones.title: A person with paralysis uses an implanted BCI at home without researcher assistance.
milestones.criterion: A person with paralysis uses the implant at home to compose a message or operate a computer without a researcher’s help. A caregiver may position hardware, connect components and start the equipment before the user takes control.
milestones.set_by: Clinical convention of researcher-independent home use, defined in the Utrecht Neural Prosthesis protocol and applied in implanted BCI home studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: the patient will be able to use it at home without the aid of researchers or other experts (but with minimal caregiver assistance).

milestones.title: A pivotal BCI study demonstrates clinically and statistically significant benefit for home use.
milestones.criterion: A pivotal clinical study demonstrates clinically and statistically significant benefit for the intended home communication and computer-control indication, meeting its prespecified safety and effectiveness success criteria. FDA recommends at least one year of follow-up for implanted BCIs. Endpoints, clinically important differences, sample size and statistical decision rules are device-specific; the guidance supplies no universal numerical performance cutoff.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Design Considerations for Pivotal Clinical Investigations for Medical Devices, supplemented by its implanted BCI guidance. These are recommendations; numerical success criteria belong to the individual protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: Studies should be designed to show both clinical and statistical significance.

milestones.title: Implanted electrodes record cortical activity at acute and chronic time points in an animal study.
milestones.criterion: Record cortical activity at acute and chronic time points and evaluate signal quality at both. For an implant intended for long-term recording, the study duration and endpoints depend on the device, its risks and the available evidence.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, implanted BCI guidance, section III.N.2, recommendations for animal study protocols where applicable.
milestones.threshold_quote: Recording signal quality at both acute and chronic timepoints (if applicable)

not_found: No field-wide minimum communication rate or maximum error rate defining completion was found in FDA guidance or NIDCD planning documents.
No published pivotal result or public pivotal protocol with numerical success criteria for combined home communication and computer control was found for the three platforms.
No FDA marketing approval for that combined home-use indication was identified in searches of FDA and developer publications.

results.detail: The release gives no cursor-specific performance number.
results.quote: Neural signals recorded from implanted electrode arrays in the speech motor cortex of the brain were decoded in real time into text and cursor control.

results.finding: One participant with severe paralysis from ALS used an intracortical BCI at home for more than 3,800 hours.
results.detail: The 3,800-hour figure is total system use. Care partners needed training to operate the system independently.
results.quote: The findings demonstrate that intracortical BCIs can provide stable, high-performance communication without researcher assistance over extended periods.

results.finding: BrainGate2, with 1 participant reported here, received FDA IDE G090003 and approvals from 2 named site IRBs.

results.quote: we showed that the participant could control the avatar BCI to portray the articulatory movements

results.finding: One participant with severe paralysis generated text with a cortical-surface BCI at home, at a median 78.3 words per minute in prompted testing.
results.detail: The reported rate applies to the prompted evaluation. The separate freeform demonstration shows self-initiated speech attempts within the research setup.
results.quote: We carried out all data collection and real-time decoding tasks in the common area of the participant’s residence.

results.finding: BrainGate’s US pilot began under FDA IDE and IRB approvals, with 1 participant enrolled and implanted by September 2004.
results.detail: The study team reported the approvals in a conference poster.
results.quote:
An open-label, 12-month, longitudinal, feasibility clinical 
study of the BrainGate™ Neural Interface System 
(Cyberkinetics, Inc.) was initiated, under Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA) Investigational Device Exemption 
(IDE) and Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals, 
in May 2004.

results.finding: One participant with quadriplegia used BrainGate’s neural cursor to select intended targets significantly more often than unintended targets in 7 of 8 sessions.
results.detail: The comparison used a one-sided z-test at alpha 0.01. Safety monitoring included connector checks, nurse visits and physician exams.
results.quote:
In 7/8 sessions, the patient’s 
neural cursor selected 
significantly more intended 
targets than false 
positive/unintended targets.

results.finding: The BrainGate2 pilot had FDA IDE approval and IRB permission from 4 named institutions.
results.quote: Permission for these studies was granted by the US Food and Drug Administration (Investigational Device Exemption) and the Institutional Review Boards of Stanford University, Providence Veterans Affairs Medical Center, Brown University, and Massachusetts General Hospital.

results.finding: Three participants with tetraplegia used neural cursor movement and clicks to operate 7 tablet apps.
results.detail: The implant supplied both pointer movement and clicks. The study reports technical performance during tablet use.
results.quote: All three participants successfully used seven common computer applications on three separate days each.

results.finding: Three participants with tetraplegia operated a tablet after technician setup across 3 research days each.
results.detail: The protocol included decoder calibration and tablet pairing. Researchers also served as correspondents during interactive tasks.
results.quote: Aside from ensuring that the cursor was active and under iBCI control by the participant, the technician did not otherwise intervene during tablet use.

results.finding: Nick (n=1) exceeded 10 bits per second using the implanted BCI for computer target selection.
results.detail: The enrollment and safety figures are reported across Neuralink’s trials. The update does not specify which participants contributed to the safety count or their follow-up duration.
results.quote: For instance, Nick achieved over 10 BPS within his first week of using the BCI.

results.finding: Noland (n=1) reportedly used Telepathy to operate a computer independently for study.
results.detail: The article mentions Noland returning home after his injury, but gives no location for the later computer use it describes.
results.quote: Being able to control a computer with full independence, Noland began waking up early, studying math, reading, and even learning new languages.

results.finding: One participant with severe paralysis drove online speech synthesis and text decoding from cortical surface signals in 80-ms increments.
results.detail: During the online demonstration, the participant silently attempted to say visually cued sentences, and the system displayed the decoded text and streamed personalized speech.
results.quote: This model emits acoustic speech units and text encodings at 80-ms increments, which are then simultaneously synthesized into personalized speech and decoded text.

results.finding: The authors report FDA IDE authorization for COMMAND, a six-participant study of Synchron’s endovascular BCI.
results.detail: The evidence is a conference abstract by the investigators. It cites the trial registration and IDE identifiers.
results.quote:
The COMMAND study (ClinicalTrials.gov registration: NCT05035823) 
was a prospective, multi-center, single-arm, open l abel, early feasibility study (EFS) conducted under  an 
investigational device exemption (G210178).

results.finding: Four of six COMMAND participants with severe paralysis used Synchron’s endovascular BCI to perform digital device control tasks.
results.detail: Rapid ALS progression affected one participant’s ability to use the system. Signal artifacts affected another.
results.quote:
Four out of six 
participants demonstrated consistent BCI decoding p erformance, enabling them to successfully perform 
various digital device control tasks throughout the  one-year post-implant evaluation period.

results.finding: In 3 rhesus macaques with 4 intracortical Utah arrays, cortical recording and signal-quality assessment spanned 382 recording days.
results.detail: Day-one spike amplitudes provided an acute baseline. Offline decoding used threshold crossings and was evaluated during periods with comparable reaching tasks.
results.quote: Here, we quantify action potential changes and offline neural decoder performance over 382 days of recording from 4 intracortical arrays in 3 animals.

results.finding: In two cynomolgus monkeys with subdural cortical surface electrodes, root mean square signal voltage fell roughly 20–40% from the acute to the chronic assessment.
results.detail: The researchers repeated the same auditory and ketamine tests at both time points. At the chronic assessment, one electrode per array gave an abnormal or unclear response. Testing took place at two discrete time points.
results.quote: In summary, the implants saw a roughly 20–40% reduction in their RMS after 15 months.

results.finding: Endovascular stentrodes in a 10-sheep cohort maintained resting cortical EEG bandwidth through 190 days.
results.detail: The 10 sheep formed the overall bandwidth cohort. The final time bin contained 8 recording channels. Wire fractures limited recordings in the separate evoked-potential cohort to 28 days.
results.quote:
The maximum 
bandwidth was stable up to 190 d: 197.4 o 42.0 H z (mea n o s.d.;  
n = 132) for 0−2 weeks and 196.4 o 20.7 Hz ( n = 8) for longer than  
20 weeks (Fig. 6).

results.finding: The BrainGate intracortical microelectrode pilot (n = 2 reported) received FDA IDE approval and approval from four IRBs.
results.detail: The Methods report both types of approval and describe screening before implantation. The approval dates, complete site coverage, and device-specific risk controls in the approved protocol are unspecified.
results.quote:
Approval for these studies was granted by the US Food and Drug Adminis-
tration (Investigational Device Exemption) and the Rhode Island Hospital, New
England, Rehabilitation Institute of Chicago, University of Chicago, and
Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital Institutional Review Boards.

results.finding: Two of two participants with ALS-related paralysis used an implanted endovascular Stentrode to operate a computer at home without researcher assistance.
results.detail: Researchers assisted with initial training. For unsupervised home use, a caregiver attached the chest receiver and launched the software. Participants then controlled the cursor by eye tracking and clicked using the implant.
results.quote: The current study achieved unsupervised home use of multiple-click actions within 86 days (participant 1) and 71 days (participant 2) of neurointerventional surgery.

definition = "Implanted electrodes record brain activity as a person with severe paralysis tries to speak or move. Software converts those signals into text, synthesized speech or computer commands. A user can, for example, point with an eye tracker and click with a brain signal. One participant has used an investigational system for both communication and computer control at home. The goal is an implant approved for those home uses, with any required assistance specified.". Reason: The definition leaves unclear what the user does, how neural and conventional inputs can work together, and how the goal differs from demonstrated home use.

goal.need = "In a US survey of 216 people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), 36 reported being unable to speak. One man with ALS typed 6.3 words per minute with a head mouse. Eye tracking can also become unreliable as voluntary eye control declines. A person who can still produce a reliable brain signal can converse with family, send email and use a computer for work at home. A caregiver may still need to position the equipment and turn it on.". Reason: The current paragraph mentions communication rates without giving one and leaves out the scale of speech loss, the practical benefit and the help home use can require.

add statement by National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, cooperative agreement U01DC016686, 2018: "develop faster and more versatile BCI control techniques for home use". Reason: The cooperative agreement explicitly connects an implanted interface for home use with both computer access and communication.

add milestone after None: "Implanted electrodes record cortical activity at acute and chronic time points in an animal study.". Reason: The sequence starts at human-study authorization and buries the earlier laboratory demonstration of sustained neural recording inside that criterion.

edit m1: title = "FDA and the site\u2019s institutional review board authorize the implant\u2019s first US study in people."; criterion = "For a significant-risk US study, the sponsor obtains FDA approval of an investigational device exemption and approval of the investigation from the institutional review board at each participating site before the study begins. The evidence from prior investigations and the risk controls are specific to the device."; threshold_quote = "Studies of devices that pose a significant risk require both FDA and an Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval prior to initiation of a clinical study."; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6, 5].
